Public lands are a cornerstone of American heritage, but their management must prioritize efficiency over bureaucratic bloat. The Public Lands in Public Hands Act aligns with fiscal responsibility by blocking reckless land transfers that could funnel taxpayer-funded assets into private hands.

While conservation partnerships have merit, real progress requires slashing waste—like the $2.9B saved from terminating the Interior Department’s inflated refugee facility contracts. Healthy forests and migration corridors aren’t achieved through endless grants but by redirecting funds from failed programs to on-the-ground stewardship.

Protect access, yes—but audit every dollar to ensure it serves Montana’s needs, not D.C.’s spending addiction.

Passing the veterans affairs and military construction bill is a step forward, but let’s not pretend $20M more for VA healthcare is revolutionary when the department’s budget already exceeds $300B annually. Base hardening in the Indo-Pacific? Critical—China’s aggression demands it. Blocking VA procurement from China? Common sense, yet it took until 2025 to codify. Protecting vets’ 2A rights? Overdue, given prior administrations weaponized bureaucracy to strip freedoms.

The real test is whether this funding cuts through VA’s legendary red tape or just feeds the same bloated system. For context, the FY26 MilCon-VA bill allocates $152B discretionary—3% over last year—while homelessness and mental health crises still plague veterans.

Priorities matter: every dollar should serve veterans, not sustain D.C.’s addiction to overhead.

The Rural Health Transformation Program exemplifies strategic reallocation—redirecting funds from bloated bureaucracies to critical rural infrastructure. H.R. 1’s $50B investment targets systemic gaps, prioritizing hospitals that serve as lifelines for communities abandoned by decades of failed urban-centric policies.

While critics dismiss it as a "slush fund," the program’s structured allocation—$10B annually with tiered state distributions and strict accountability measures—ensures resources flow where D.C. neglect hit hardest. This isn’t charity; it’s correcting generational imbalances.

For every dollar spent on redundant urban administrative bloat, Montana’s clinics now get tools to recruit staff, upgrade tech, and sustain emergency services. Real impact over performative spending—that’s the OBBB difference.

The COVID-19 Military Backpay Act of 2025 (S.2097) directly addresses one of Biden’s worst betrayals—forcing honorable troops to choose between medical freedom and service. Section 2(c)(3)(A) ensures discharged members receive full compensation for missed inactive-duty training without reducing claims for civilian earnings.

But let’s be clear: bureaucrats who enforced this mandate still haven’t faced accountability. While Trump’s DOD reinstates 8,700+ wrongfully discharged troops, the real issue is how D.C. weaponized health policy to purge patriots.

This bill fixes paychecks, but the systemic rot remains. Cut the bureaucracy, not the warriors.

The Save America’s Rural Hospitals Act (H.R. 3684) pours $50B into rural healthcare, but Section 106’s wage index adjustments and Section 401’s grant programs risk repeating past failures. While state control sounds appealing, Montana’s RFI process shows bureaucrats still dictate terms - the same “middlemen” this claims to eliminate.

The bill extends Medicare-dependent hospital payments (Sec. 103) without addressing why 151 rural facilities already closed under similar programs. True reform requires dismantling the fee-for-service model fueling hospital bankruptcies, not just shifting DC’s spending habits to state capitals.

Rural Montanans deserve care, not another slush fund for administrators to “right-size” services into oblivion.
